3.0.s.en: 1. The works of God through the years:

3.0.0.en: "1 A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth (strings): 2 O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid.

3.0.1.en: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy" [1-2].

3.0.2.en: When the prophet stood on the watchtower awaiting the word of God, and took his stand on the divine tower, taking refuge, his soul rejoiced within him in spite of all the harsh circumstances surrounding him. And while the prophet was groaning for the sake of the people of God, God revealed to him His plan of salvation through the ages, which was manifested on the Cross, so he rejoiced, taking hold of the harp of the Spirit to strike its strings with a psalm of praise, saying:

3.0.3.en: "O LORD, I have heard thy speech (thy word), and was afraid." It is as though he says: O Lord, when I heard Your word my soul was filled with awe and fear; You revealed Your mysteries to me and I understood Your works, and I was amazed!

3.0.4.en: His vision did not stop at the limits of God's works in his own age, but extended to see them through the ages, realizing that God in His love, though He is angry and disciplines, yet even in His anger cannot bear the groaning of His people, but returns and has mercy. "O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy." Truly the Lord is angry at the evil of man, but in the midst of His anger His mercies groan, a matter that the prophet Hosea expressed in a wonderful image, saying on the tongue of the Lord: "Mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together. I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath" (Hos 11:8-9).

3.0.5.en: Although God is a hidden God, or one who hides Himself, as Isaiah the prophet said (Isa 45:15), He reveals Himself to His people through the generations by His mercies, which He shows even in moments of divine anger and discipline... Perhaps what God presents through the years in the way of revelations is shown in practice in the change of humanity that had been corrupted and which He raised from its fall. As St. Jerome says: [God works wonders every day; He is at work... You are the wonderful works of God; yesterday you were seizing what belonged to others, and today you give to others what is yours". This change is the goal of the word of God revealed through the Mosaic Law, which was manifested in its fullness through the incarnation of the divine Word and His declaration of salvation on the Cross. For this reason the prophet returns to the works of God with His people in the wilderness, with the giving of the Law on Mount Moses, in order to proceed with them to His works through the Messiah the Savior.

3.1.s.en: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

3.1.0.en: 3 God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. 4 And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power. 5 Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet. 6 He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting. 7 I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble. 8 Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation? 9 Thy bow was made quite naked, the sevenfold arrows are thy word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers. 10 The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high. 11 The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear. 12 Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.

3.1.1.en: The heart of the prophet Habakkuk was drawn to the work of God when Moses went up on the mountain to receive the Law, and the mountain was filled with splendor and glory, and God shone with His light upon His people, so that his heart and tongue, his soul and body, were set free in joy and praise, saying:

3.1.2.en: "God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah.

3.1.3.en: His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise" [3].

3.1.4.en: He points here to the appearance of God in His glory in a tangible way when Moses received the Law, as it is said: "The LORD came down upon mount Sinai" (Ex 19:20), "And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like devouring fire on the top of the mount" (Ex 24:17), "The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran" (Deut 33:2).

3.1.5.en: When He came to us through the Law, His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was filled with His praise. What are these heavens and earth if not the human soul and body, which are sanctified by the word of God, so that the soul shines with the glory of the Lord and the body is filled with joy and exultation? Through the divine Word the soul is filled with divine light and heavenly knowledge, while the body, with all its members, is turned into a harp in the hands of the Holy Spirit, on which He plays a unique, heavenly hymn. In other words, God is manifested in the whole of man's life, in his soul as in his body. St. Jerome says: [Sing true praise; sing psalms with every part of your being. Let your hand sing by giving, and your foot by hastening to do good... Let all your strings give a sound, for if one string stops the harp loses its being. What does it profit you if you are chaste but covetous?! What do you gain if you are pure and generous in giving but at the same time envious?! What is your benefit if six of your strings are sound and the seventh is broken?! For one broken string deprives the harp of its ability to give a complete sound].

3.1.6.en: In the Septuagint it reads: "God cometh from the south, and the Holy One from the shady mountain," and St. Jerome comments on this phrase: "God comes from the south. Here he points to the Savior, for God was born in the south, because Bethlehem is south of Jerusalem." St. Didymus the Blind sees that the south points to the hot winds that blow upon the soul and inflame it with the Spirit, or with love, so that it is not cold, while the north points to the cold northern winds, which point to the work of Satan, who spoils the warmth of the Spirit; therefore in the Song of Songs the bride asked that the north wind, which is the work of the devil, be removed from her, and that the south wind come to her, which points to the Savior, her Bridegroom Himself.

3.2.0.en: The prophet continues his hymn, saying: "And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power" [4]. It is as though he says: I used to think that matters went on without direction, the wicked devouring the righteous, and the nation of the Chaldeans swallowing the rest of the peoples, with no one to call it to account and no one to restrain it; but when I understood the mysteries of Your knowledge, I found You to be the eternal Light who comprehends hidden mysteries, with nothing hidden from Your eyes. You stretch out Your hand to work, and a ray comes forth from it that exposes those who walk in darkness; then all understand Your power, which was hidden for a time.

3.2.1.en: The phrase "he had horns coming out of his hand" means the light of the rays of the sun, as it appears in the translation of the Jesuits. These two horns in His hand are the two tables of the Law, which the prophet Moses received, as it is said: "from his right hand went a fiery law for them" (Deut 23:2).

3.3.0.en: "Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals (fever) went forth at his feet" [5].

3.3.1.en: By His appearing He drives out the pestilence of evil and darkness, and at His feet, that is, with authority, He commands the fever and it obeys Him.

3.4.0.en: "He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting" [6].

3.4.1.en: He stands to measure the earth, for it is His creation for which He cares; for its sake He stands to work and does not rest until He declares His judgments, so that the wicked nations tremble and the lofty mountains and the ancient hills are crushed. He is the Everlasting One who orders all things to work in the good time. It is as though he says: I used to think the world was like a sea full of fish that the wicked nation hunts without restraint, but I have realized that nothing is hidden from You.

3.4.2.en: If the earth, as we said before, points to the body, then God stood to measure it as a sign of His care for it and His sanctifying it, so that the pagan nations dwelling there tremble, that is, every evil and spiritual weakness is removed from the body, and the lofty mountains are crushed, that is, the sins that seem extremely violent, which no one can move. Before God the hills of the body that weigh down the soul are shaken.

3.4.3.en: Here the prophet describes God as standing: "He stood, and measured the earth." As St. Jerome says: [God does not change and has no bodily postures, but He is said to stand when He deals with the righteous, and He is said to appear walking when Adam fell (Gen 3:9), and sitting as Judge and King (Isa 6:1), and sleeping, as in the boat, when man is amid the storms of temptation, and He appears standing, as it is said, "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty." He is therefore speaking here of the earth, which has enjoyed the gladness of His salvation and has been sanctified by it, so He appeared standing to measure it!

3.5.0.en: I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble" [7].

3.5.1.en: The name "tents of Cushan" is not mentioned in the Old Testament except in this phrase; it may be an ancient name for Midian that was abandoned. Thus, if the vision of God is manifested to Habakkuk, and the Lord in his eyes is coming from Mount Sinai, then everything that resists Him collapses before Him.

3.5.2.en: Perhaps the tents of Cushan appeared as though under affliction and the curtains of Midian trembling when God gave the land of Canaan to His people, and all the surrounding nations trembled.

3.5.3.en: Some think that the tents of Cushan came under affliction when the Lord delivered Cushan into the hand of the judge Othniel the son of Kenaz after Israel had served him eight years (Judg 3:8-11), and the power of God was manifested in His judge sent for the salvation of His people, and He humbled the one who had enslaved His people. As for the trembling of the curtains of Midian, it happened when the companion of Gideon saw a dream: "a cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian, and came unto a tent, and smote it that it fell, and overturned it, that the tent lay along" (Judg 7:3), and that was a sign of the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, who slew the Midianites.

3.5.4.en: In short, Habakkuk praises the Lord for His works, in that He gives His children victory and triumph, and even authority, so that the demons tremble before them and come under affliction!

3.6.0.en: "Was the LORD displeased against the rivers?! was thine anger against the rivers, or thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?!" [8].

3.6.1.en: If many waters point to peoples (Rev 17:15), then the people of God are likened to rivers, where the water is sweet, and the pagan nations to the salt seas. When God disciplines His people, His anger is kindled against the rivers because of the injustice found in their midst, and when He punishes the nations in His wrath because of the evils they committed against His people, His anger is kindled against the seas.

3.6.2.en: His anger was kindled against the rivers and seas when they stood in the way of His people in their crossing from the land of Egypt to the Promised Land, so He divided the Red Sea and the River Jordan, passing through with His people as with chariots of salvation, as though He were the leader of the procession of salvation that brings them across from the slavery of the devil to His heavenly Kingdom, while the believers are the horses who carry God, their Leader, within them. St. Jerome says in this regard: [This is said of God, if we are the horses of God on which He rides]. And Father Theophan the Recluse says: [He fights for you Himself, and delivers your enemies into your hands whenever He wills, however He wills, as it is written: "For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee" (Deut 23:4)].

3.7.0.en: "Thy bow was made quite naked, the sevenfold arrows are thy words. Selah" [9].

3.7.1.en: What is the bow that was made naked to strike like sevenfold arrows, if not the divine Incarnation, through which we enjoyed the Word of God as an arrow that shatters the evil that had reigned within us?! May the Word of God dwell in us as a true arrow that wounds our hearts with love, so that we say, "I am sick of love" (Song 2:5), and removes from them all the malignant corruption which the wicked enemy established in them.

3.7.2.en: The words of the Lord are "sevenfold"; they enter the heart and make it perfect, for the number 7 points to perfection.

3.7.3.en: "Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers" [9].

3.7.4.en: When we receive the incarnate Word in us as a divine arrow that wounds our hearts with love and removes their corruption, He in turn, seeing that they have become earth and not heaven, loving the temporal rather than the eternal, cleaves it through fellowship in the Cross and suffering, and turns the earth into rivers of living water, as the Savior said: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38).

3.7.5.en: Let us not fear that we are a barren land, for the Lord by His Cross causes the springs of His Holy Spirit to burst forth in us like rivers of living water, which water our land and overflow with witness to Him in every place!

3.7.6.en: St. Jerome sees that the Lord Christ is the original River who pours into our land rivers that are the fruit of His work in us; these rivers bear witness to the true River, praising Him not by words only but also by deeds, as the Psalmist says: "Let the floods clap their hands" (Ps 98:8). "May the rivers that are watered from the Source, Jesus, clap their hands, for the work of the saints is the praise of God. Christ is not praised by words but by deeds; He asks for action, not for voice."

3.8.0.en: "The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high" [10].

3.8.1.en: If the living Word of God cleaves our earth by His Cross and makes it rivers of water that praise Him and sing to Him by true spiritual work, then, in His dwelling within us, the mountains of our heavy sins see Him and flee in fear from before His face. What we used to count as firm mountains that no one could move become, by the Cross, a plain. As it is said in Zechariah: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings among the shouters, honor, honor to it" (Zech 4:7). We have seen in our study of the book of Zechariah how the evil mountain disappears so that the Lord Christ appears as the cornerstone, the honored One, cut out without hands, since He is not of the seed of man, and becomes a mountain that fills the whole earth (Dan 2:35). By this the grace of God flows like boundless waters to give a voice of inner praise, and the two inner hands of the soul are lifted on high to practice the heavenly work.

3.8.2.en: "The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear. Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.

3.8.3.en: Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed" [11-13].

3.8.4.en: As the prophet praises God for His works through the years, he recalls the days of Joshua, when he prayed that the sun and moon should stand still in their places in heaven until Israel's victory over its enemies was completed (Josh 10:12-13), so that no swift night should come in which the enemy would flee before the defeat was accomplished. In the light Joshua defeated the enemy, and so, when the Lord shines in the heart as the Sun of Righteousness, and the battlefield is turned into a moon, being the holy Church that resists the devil, the light scatters the darkness of the enemy, and the Lord remains shining until the victory is completely achieved.

3.8.5.en: Perhaps he also means that all nature is subject to God's work of salvation, so that even the sun and moon work together according to His plan to establish His kingdom of light and destroy the kingdom of darkness.

3.8.6.en: We can say that "the sun and moon stood still in their habitation" on the day of the Cross, when they vanished before the splendor of the glory of the Sun of Righteousness, in shame at what humanity was doing to Him. They stood hidden, astonished also at how the Lord Christ shatters the devil and all his hosts to free man from them as from pagan nations, saying: "In anger thou didst thresh the heathen; thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thine anointed."

3.9.0.en: 13 Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah. 14 Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly. 15 Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters. 16 When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops. 17 Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: 18 Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. 19 The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places.

3.9.1.en: "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed.

3.9.2.en: Thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.

3.9.3.en: Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages" [13-14].

3.9.4.en: The prophet concludes his hymn by revealing God's salvation for man, by shattering the devil's authority over us and by raising up the spirit of joy in us. By the Cross He crushed the head of the house of the wicked devil, which was laid bare down to the foundation, and his hidden deceits appeared, exposing him from the foundation to the neck. If the enemy aimed his arrows against us, it was only so that they would turn back upon him and shatter him completely, so that he would have no authority over us and no place in us.

3.9.5.en: The Fathers have often spoken to us about the shattering of the devil's authority in order to raise in us hope for spiritual work without fear or wavering. Among their words:

3.9.6.en: * On the Cross Christ put Satan and all his army to shame. Be sure that Christ was crucified in His body on the Cross, and by it He crucified Satan there... The Cross was a sign of victory and a banner of triumph. His purpose in being lifted up on the Cross was to lift us up from the earth, and as I think, the Cross of the Savior is the ladder that Jacob saw.

3.9.7.en: St. Jerome * We learn the art of war so that we can struggle not against men but against spirits. Indeed, if we had a (true) mind we would never struggle; we struggle because we have chosen this, although we have received authority from the One who dwells in us, who said, "Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy" (Lk 10:19). He has given you all authority to struggle or not to struggle, if you wish. We struggle because we are slack, but the Apostle Paul did not struggle; rather he says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Rom 8:35). Listen also to his words: "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20). He bore authority when he said: "I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her" (Acts 16:18). This is not the language of one who struggles, for he who struggles has not yet conquered, and he who conquers no longer struggles.

3.9.8.en: * If we wish, God makes him trodden under our feet, but what contempt and misery it is to see him tread on the heads of those to whom it was given to trample him under their feet?! How does this happen?! It is because of us. If we wish, he is great, and if we wish, he is of little cunning. If we are watchful and stand beside our King, he withdraws, and in his war against us he is no more than a little child.

3.9.9.en: St. John Chrysostom This is the secret of the joy of the prophet's soul, when he saw God's saving work in shattering the devil's authority for the sake of the kingdom of light. Truly his inward parts trembled when he saw the Chaldeans spoiling all fruit, but behind this discipline there is a greater good, when God turns discipline into the joy of salvation.

3.10.0.en: The prophet says: "When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops" [16]. He saw the Chaldeans as a people who crowd upon them or as an enemy who wishes to destroy them, so his belly trembled, his lips quivered, and rottenness entered into his bones... The enemy has spoiled all spiritual fruit, so the fig tree does not blossom and the vines bear no fruit, and the olive trees have dried up. This is the picture of man fallen under the devil, who does not enjoy the unity of the Spirit (the fig tree), nor the work of the Cross (the vines that are pressed), nor inner peace (the olive); that is, he loses his inner life by being deprived of the work of the Holy Spirit and of attachment to the Cross of our Lord Jesus. And the matter does not stop at the corruption of the inner depths, but even the body loses its holiness and becomes like dead animals, for he says: "and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls" [17]. The body finds no spiritual food, so it hungers and falls ill and even dies spiritually, and man becomes like a fold without flock and a stall without herd! This is what the enemy desires, the loss of the holiness of the soul and also of the body.

3.10.1.en: But God does not leave man thus; rather, He restores his salvation to him, giving him the joy of salvation, offering Himself as his strength, and making his feet firm to run toward heaven swiftly like hinds, so that man walks upon the holy heights and does not descend into the mire of the world and its dust, for he says:

3.11.0.en: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments" [18-19].

3.11.1.en: Thus the book began with pain and distress with bitterness because of inner and outer troubles, but when the prophet entered into an open dialogue with God and stood as on a watchtower awaiting, and on a fortress taking his stand to see the works of God, the book ended with joy and gladness, as he realized that God Himself is the strength of His children, who strengthens their feet and lifts them to the heights to carry them by His Holy Spirit above all events.
